comments.issue_title: UDP inbound silently drops bursts: per-session pipe hardcoded to 16 KiB with DiscardOverflow (WireGuard over tunnel/dokodemo collapses to ~1 Mbps)
comments.body:
Thanks for the independent measurement. It fills two gaps in my report: a before/after at the stock 16 KiB, and the confirmation that `XRAY_RAY_BUFFER_SIZE` doesn't reach this code path.

To follow up on that, I reran it as a controlled A/B that also reproduces the ~1 Mbps figure.

**Setup:** v26.10.21 with drop counters added (no other change), in Docker on an arm64 host. The path matches my real one: kernel WG (MTU 1280) → `tunnel` UDP inbound → VLESS + REALITY + Vision → freedom → WG → iperf3. The WAN between the two containers is netem with 100 ms each way and 50 Mbit. Both sides have `rmem_default/max` = 32 MiB, as on my production hosts. The inner sender is CUBIC, doing 15 s uploads. Pipe size and hub capacity are set through env overrides, so the arm64 policy default doesn't come into it.

| WAN loss | pipe / hub cap | Mbps | pipe drops | hub drops | kernel `RcvbufErrors` |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 16 KiB / 256 (stock) | 1.5, 1.3 | 40, 90 | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 MiB / 1024 | 39.3, 39.8 | 302, 1101 ¹ | 0 | 0 |
| 0.1% | 16 KiB / 256 (stock) | 1.0, 1.0, 1.5 | 36, 42, 40 | 0 | 0 |
| 0.1% | 512 KiB / 256 | 12.4, 17.0, 16.7 | 0, 325, 866 | 0, 0, 537 | 0 |
| 0.1% | 1 MiB / 256 | 17.3, 14.6, 16.8 | 4, 0, 0 | 173, 0, 265 | 0 |
| 0.1% | 1 MiB / 1024 | 5.7, 12.0, 8.0 ² | 0 | 0 | 0 |

¹ This run saturates the 50 Mbit line. These drops are the normal congestion signal at the bottleneck. At 16 KiB, drops start far below line rate.
² The spread in the 0.1% rows comes from the outer connection. The container kernel has no BBR, so the outer TCP runs CUBIC over a lossy 200 ms path. Production uses BBR there.

What it shows:

- **The two drop points account for all the loss.** In every run, the inner TCP retransmits equal pipe drops + hub drops (e.g. 1403 = 866 + 537, 177 = 4 + 173). WG byte counters on both ends agree to the packet.
- **WAN loss isn't needed to trigger it.** With a clean WAN, stock 16 KiB holds a single CUBIC flow at ~1.3 Mbps. That's the same as my real path (1.3–2.0 Mbps), so the ~1 Mbps figure comes from the inner TCP reacting to these drops, not from anything else on the path.
- **The hub queue is the next bottleneck.** After the pipe is raised, the loss moves to the hub's 256-entry queue. Only raising both brings it to zero, so I think a fix needs to cover `hub.go:37` as well, not just `worker.go`.
- **The kernel socket buffer is a third drop point, but it's visible.** With the default `rmem` (~224 KiB), raising the pipe moves the loss into the kernel socket buffer (`RcvbufErrors`). That one at least shows up in a counter. It's why my production hosts showed 0 there.

I'm the reporter, not a maintainer, so whether a PR is accepted is up to the maintainers. On the design, I agree with all three of your points:

1. **Floor.** Something like `max(policy, 16 KiB)`, so arm64/arm/mips never end up worse than today.
2. **Ceiling.** `0` means unlimited, so clamp it. In the runs above, 512 KiB–1 MiB was the useful range.
3. **Keep `DiscardOverflow`.** Agreed. Backpressure in the shared `handlePackets` goroutine would stall every session on the inbound.

I'd add two things. The hub capacity should get a matching change, since it's per inbound rather than per session, so a larger fixed value or one scaled from the same policy seems fine. And the drops should be counted somehow (a stats counter, or at least a rate-limited debug log), in both places. Being invisible is what made this so hard to find.

On who writes the PR: my local patch (env-configurable pipe size and hub capacity, plus drop counters) was for debugging, and your policy-based approach with a floor and ceiling fits upstream better. If you want to send it, go ahead. I'm happy to run it through this setup and post the same table. If you'd rather not, I can send one based on your design. Either way, I'll wait for a maintainer to say which knob they prefer. I can also share the compose files if that would help with review.

issues.title: fix(windows): unblock WireGuard connect with large split-tunnel lists
issues.body:
Fixes #2248.

Currently, when connecting to a WireGuard server on Windows with a large split-tunnel list (e.g. the 11k-CIDR RU list from #2248), the client spends 5–20 minutes on "Connecting" before it finally reports "Connected". The same profile connects in 1–3 seconds on macOS, Android and iOS. Even after the first connect succeeds, reconnecting in the same session hangs on "Connecting" indefinitely.

This happens because `Daemon::activate` installs exclusion routes one at a time: every `CreateIpForwardEntry2` call wakes `wcmSvc` (which `router_win.cpp` already works around for OpenVPN/Shadowsocks but not for WireGuard), and `WindowsRouteMonitor::addExclusionRoute` re-fetches the full routing table and re-runs `updateCapturedRoutes` for every prefix. On top of that, `NotifyRouteChange2` fires a callback per row during interface bring-up; each callback queues a `routeChanged` slot that rescans everything, and Wintun's subnet-broadcast `/32` entries (which `QHostAddress::isBroadcast()` does not recognize) keep failing with `ERROR_OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` and get retried on every rescan - the daemon event loop fills up and `Daemon::checkHandshake()` never gets a slot, so the `connected` signal never reaches the GUI.

This PR adds batch entry points to `WireguardUtils` so `WindowsRouteMonitor` can install all exclusion prefixes against one routing-table snapshot per address family and suspend `wcmSvc` for the whole batch (matching `router_win.cpp`), debounces `NotifyRouteChange2` callbacks through a 50 ms single-shot timer so bursts collapse into one rescan, and pins prefixes that return `ERROR_OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` so they stop being retried. Other platforms fall back to the existing per-prefix path and are untouched.

Update: disconnect/reconnect and server switch now also remove routes in one batch with wcmSvc suspended, and a gateway change no longer rewrites all exclusion routes with wcmSvc running. Also fixes: routes covered by a removed exclusion were not re-captured (inverted check in updateCapturedRoutes), a colliding prefix stayed outside the tunnel permanently, and switchServer did not remove CIDR exclusions of the previous server.

Happens on most connects, especially noticeable right after the first connection attempt.

**Root cause**
AmneziaVPN restarts `systemd-resolved` and immediately tries to configure DNS on amn0 via DBus. The service hasn't fully initialized its DBus interface yet, so the call fails silently and DNS is never set on amn0.

Visible in `/var/log/AmneziaVPN/AmneziaVPN-service.log` right after connect:
```
[DEBUG] Amnezia  : Restarting systemd-resolved.service
[DEBUG] Amnezia  : Flush dns completed
[ERROR] Amnezia DnsUtilsLinux : Error retrieving the DNS domains from the DBus service
[ERROR] Amnezia DnsUtilsLinux : Error received from the DBus service
[ERROR] Amnezia DnsUtilsLinux : Error received from the DBus service
```

**Workaround**
Note: `systemctl restart systemd-resolved` hangs when resolved is stuck — use `kill` + `start` instead.

Manual fix (run after connecting when DNS doesn't work):
```bash
sudo systemctl kill systemd-resolved
sudo systemctl start systemd-resolved

for i in $(seq 1 15); do
    busctl status org.freedesktop.resolve1 &>/dev/null && break
    sleep 1
done

sudo resolvectl dns amn0 8.8.8.8 1.0.0.1
sudo resolvectl domain amn0 "~."
```

Permanent automated fix — udev rule that triggers a systemd service on amn0 creation:

`/etc/udev/rules.d/99-amnezia-dns.rules`:
```
ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEM=="net", KERNEL=="amn0", TAG+="systemd", ENV{SYSTEMD_WANTS}="amnezia-fix-dns.service"
```

`/etc/systemd/system/amnezia-fix-dns.service`:
```ini
[Unit]
Description=Fix AmneziaVPN DNS on amn0
After=systemd-resolved.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/amnezia-fix-dns.sh
```

`/usr/local/bin/amnezia-fix-dns.sh`:
```bash
#!/bin/bash
for i in $(seq 1 15); do
    busctl status org.freedesktop.resolve1 &>/dev/null && break
    sleep 1
done
resolvectl dns amn0 8.8.8.8 1.0.0.1
resolvectl domain amn0 "~."
```

**Expected behavior**
DNS should be correctly configured on amn0 immediately after connecting.

issues.body:
# [Bug] Windows 5.0.3.0: IP Split Tunneling breaks NetBird routing

## Description

After updating to AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0, IP Split Tunneling breaks connectivity to devices on another VPN (NetBird).

**Even when the NetBird subnet is explicitly added to AmneziaVPN's exclusion list, traffic is incorrectly routed through the physical Wi-Fi gateway instead of the NetBird interface.**

As a result, SSH and other remote connections stop working.

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN: 5.0.3.0 (Windows)
- NetBird: 0.72.2
- NetBird interface: `wt0`
- Excluded subnet: `100.68.0.0/16`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Connect NetBird.
2. Enable IP Split Tunneling in AmneziaVPN.
3. Add `100.68.0.0/16` to the exclusion list.
4. Connect AmneziaVPN.
5. Check the routing table using `route print -4`.

## Actual behavior

AmneziaVPN creates conflicting routes through the physical Wi-Fi gateway:

```text
100.68.0.0/16  → Wi-Fi gateway
100.68.x.x/32  → Wi-Fi gateway
```

Instead of using the existing NetBird route:

```text
100.68.0.0/16  → wt0 (NetBird)
```

## Temporary workaround

Manually deleting the incorrect routes immediately restores SSH connectivity:

```powershell
Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 |
    Where-Object {
        $_.InterfaceAlias -eq "Wi-Fi" -and
        (
            $_.DestinationPrefix -eq "100.68.0.0/16" -or
            $_.DestinationPrefix -match '^100\.68\.\d+\.\d+/32$'
        )
    } |
    Remove-NetRoute -Confirm:$false
```

**However, the incorrect routes reappear after reconnecting AmneziaVPN or reapplying Split Tunneling settings.**

## Expected behavior

Excluded IP traffic should follow existing Windows routes, including routes through other VPN interfaces, rather than being forcibly redirected to the physical gateway.

*Note: Individual device IPs and gateway addresses have been omitted for privacy. The NetBird subnet is retained to demonstrate the routing conflict.*

issues.title: Self-hosted: optional per-config update endpoint for in-app fleet failover/rotation
issues.body:
## Summary

An optional, opt-in improvement for self-hosted users: let a `SelfHosted` config include the operator's own update endpoint together with a pinned public key, so the client can periodically pull a refreshed config from it. This gives self-hosters automatic failover / rotation across their own fleet of servers. It is purely additive and off by default.

## Problem

Self-hosting is great, but a single server occasionally goes down — the hosting provider, a block, or just a crash. So people who self-host usually run a small fleet of servers rather than one. Today the app only understands static configs: when a server goes down, the user has to manually switch between separate configs. There is no way to do failover or rotation across your own infrastructure from inside the app.

## Proposal

Add an optional field to a self-hosted config: the operator's update endpoint plus a pinned public key. When those fields are present, the client periodically fetches a refreshed config from that endpoint, verifies the response signature against the pinned key, and applies it (server list / active server / DNS, etc.). Properties:

- **opt-in** — only active when the imported config includes these fields;
- **scoped** — only for user-imported `SelfHosted` configs;
- **verified** — the response must be signed by the key pinned at import time, so a config can only ever update itself from the operator who issued it.

In practice the operator (the self-hoster) runs a tiny endpoint that returns the current best config for their fleet, and the app follows it automatically instead of the user re-importing configs by hand.

## It fits the existing code well

*(paths/lines as of tag 4.8.19.0)*

- The `SelfHosted` config type and a per-config `api_endpoint` field already exist — [apiDefs.h (ConfigType)](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/core/api/apiDefs.h#L8-L16) and [apiEndpoint key](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/core/api/apiDefs.h#L26).
- The client already knows how to fetch a config from a remote source and apply it (containers / hostName / DNS) — [fillServerConfig()](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/ui/controllers/api/apiConfigsController.cpp#L159).
- The request base URL for those fetches is a single settable value, not hardcoded at the call sites — [Settings::setGatewayEndpoint()](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/settings.cpp#L505) — so the same fetch machinery can target a per-config endpoint.
- The architecture already supports third-party operators distributing configs through the app — the external-premium / external-trial service types in [apiUtils::getConfigType()](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/core/api/apiUtils.cpp#L85-L124). A self-hoster with a fleet is the same shape: they would just point at their own control plane.

## Result

Multi-server self-hosting gets real, in-app failover and rotation across your own fleet, via a small, opt-in, signature-verified mechanism that reuses machinery already present in the client. Happy to help with a PR or a test config if the direction is interesting.

---

**Reference server implementation** (runnable, clean-room, MIT): **https://github.com/wintergenius/Fleetcore** — it speaks the exact wire format this proposal implies (`GET /v1/config` → an Ed25519-signed `vpn://…` config), so the whole loop can be run with `docker run`. Details in the comment below.

# macOS: Site-based split tunneling is not applied for AWG/WireGuard — always full tunnel

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN client: **5.0.3.0** (macOS pkg, universal)
- OS: **macOS 27.0.1** (Apple Silicon, arm64)
- Protocol: **AWG** (self-hosted server, amneziawg-tools v3.1.20260812)
- GUI state: Settings → Split tunneling → Sites → **"Only for selected sites"** (`Conf.routeMode = 1`, `Conf.ForwardSites` populated with 36 domains), VPN reconnected after the change

## Summary

On macOS, for AWG (and WireGuard) connections, the site-based split tunneling settings are **silently ignored** — the connection is always full tunnel. Two independent code paths cause this:

### 1. Route-split logic is skipped for AWG/WG containers

`client/vpnConnection.cpp` (`VpnConnection::onConnectionStateChanged`, Connected branch) wraps the **entire** split-tunneling route logic in:

```cpp
// line 135
if (!ContainerUtils::isAwgContainer(container) && container != DockerContainer::WireGuard) {
    ...
    if (m_appSettingsRepository->isSitesSplitTunnelingEnabled()) {
        // routeDeleteList("0.0.0.0"), VpnOnlyForwardSites -> addSitesRoutes(),
        // VpnAllExceptSites -> 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 ...
    }
}
```

For AWG and WireGuard containers none of this ever runs: neither forward-site routes (include mode) nor exception routes (exclude mode) are added, and the DNS servers are not excluded from the tunnel on macOS.

### 2. Client config is hardcoded to full tunnel

`client/core/configurators/wireguardConfigurator.cpp` (line 275):

```cpp
clientConfig.allowedIps = QStringList { "0.0.0.0/0", "::/0" };
```

This is unconditional — the configured split-tunneling mode is not reflected in `AllowedIPs`. The macOS daemon then expands the default route into two halves (`client/platforms/macos/daemon/wireguardutilsmacos.cpp`, `updateRoutePrefix`, line 357):

```cpp
return m_rtmonitor->insertRoute(IPAddress("0.0.0.0/1")) &&
       m_rtmonitor->insertRoute(IPAddress("128.0.0.0/1"));
```

So every AWG connection gets `0/1` + `128.0/1` → tunnel, i.e. full tunnel, regardless of GUI state.

### 3. Related: `routeGateway()` is never set for WG/AWG

`VpnProtocol::routeGateway()` is only populated by the OpenVPN (`openVpnProtocol.cpp:172,178`) and Xray (`xrayProtocol.cpp:33`) protocols. For WireGuard/AWG it stays empty. The macOS-only branch in the `VpnAllExceptSites` path relies on it:

```cpp
#ifdef Q_OS_MACOS
    iface->routeAddList(m_vpnProtocol->routeGateway(), QStringList() << dns1 << dns2);
#endif
    addSitesRoutes(m_vpnProtocol->routeGateway(), routeMode);
```

— so even for protocols where the split logic runs, on macOS the DNS exclusion routes and site routes are added via an **empty gateway** whenever the protocol is WG/AWG (`routeAddList("", ip)` silently fails).

## Steps to reproduce

1. macOS 27.0.1 (arm64), AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0, self-hosted AWG server
2. Settings → Split tunneling → Sites → mode "Only for selected sites", add e.g. `youtube.com`
3. Connect via AWG
4. `route -n get alfabank.ru` (not in the list) → `interface: utunX` (tunnel) — expected `en0`
5. `route -n get youtube.com` → `interface: utunX` — this one is correct, but only because everything is routed into the tunnel

## Actual result

- `route -n get default` → en0, but `0/1` + `128.0/1` → utun (full tunnel in practice)
- Sites **not** in the forward list (including the configured DNS servers, e.g. 1.1.1.1) are routed through the tunnel
- GUI split-tunneling settings have **no effect** on AWG connections

- "All except sites" mode cannot keep RU-local resources (banks, gov services) on the direct path — they egress via the VPN IP

issues.title: Android: auto-reconnect when the AmneziaWG tunnel stalls after idle (connection watchdog)
issues.body:
AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.1 (AWG 3.1), Android 16, OnePlus 15.
Self-hosted AmneziaWG, mobile network (Russia), battery set
to "Unrestricted" for AmneziaVPN.

Problem
After the phone has been idle with the screen off, the tunnel
sometimes stalls: nothing works (Telegram, browser) until I
manually disconnect and reconnect in AmneziaVPN. It happens
several times a day. A manual reconnect always fixes it
immediately.

What we see on the server side
We captured traffic on our server during these episodes. While
the tunnel is stalled, no packets from the phone reach the server
at all — no handshake initiation, nothing, for 4–44 minutes.
Other devices on the same server work normally at the same time.
Typical sequence: the phone wakes up, sends a few data packets
with the old session from a new NAT port (the mobile operator
changed it during sleep), the server drops them (keys older than
180 s), and then the phone never sends a new handshake. A manual
reconnect opens a new socket, the handshake completes in ~0.1 s,
and traffic flows right away.

Feature request: connection watchdog
An option to detect a stalled tunnel and restart it automatically,
for example:
- if the latest handshake is older than ~140 s
  (REKEY_AFTER_TIME + KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT + REKEY_TIMEOUT, as in
  wireguard-tools reresolve-dns) while the app has traffic to send,
  or
- if a periodic check through the tunnel (ping/HTTP) fails
  N times in a row,
then recreate the socket and re-handshake — the same as a manual
reconnect. Configurable interval and on/off switch.

Similar features exist in other clients: WG Tunnel ("Restart
tunnel on ping failure"), mihomo-based clients (fallback groups
with health checks).

Server-side keepalive does not help here: we tried
PersistentKeepalive 25 on the server for this peer — the server
cannot reach the phone after the operator's NAT mapping changes,
only the phone can recover by sending first.

Thank you for AmneziaVPN!

issues.title: fix(tproxy): send UDP packets that race the pair socket via the existing session
issues.body:
## Problem

With `udpTProxy`, QUIC to proxied destinations often never completes. Clients that use a post-quantum key share (X25519MLKEM768, the default in current Chrome/Firefox, curl + OpenSSL 3.5) send a ClientHello that spans **two datagrams**, back-to-back.

`ListenAndServe` only expects the first packet of a src/dst pair. `newPair` then dials a transparent socket that takes over the pair through `-m socket --transparent`. The second datagram arrives before that socket exists, so it also lands on the listener and `newPair` opens a **second** hysteria UDP session for the same pair. The server receives the two ClientHello halves from two different source addresses and the handshake stalls.

## Fix

The listener tracks active pairs (`sync.Map`, src/dst key). Packets for a pair that already exists go through that pair's session instead of creating a new one. `HyUDPConn.Send` is documented as not thread-safe, so sends are serialized per pair: the listener and the pair's forwarding goroutine can now both send. The entry is removed when forwarding ends, with `CompareAndDelete` so a newer pair isn't removed by mistake.

## Testing

Tested on Linux arm64 router, standard TPROXY rules (`-m socket --transparent` mark, TPROXY to the listener). Client: curl 8.14.1 / OpenSSL 3.5, `--http3-only https://quic.nginx.org/`:

| ClientHello | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `--curves X25519` (1 datagram) | 200 h3, 1 session | 200 h3, 1 session |
| `--curves X25519MLKEM768` (2 datagrams) | timeout, 2 `UDP transparent proxy connect` for the same pair | 200 h3 in ~0.15 s, 1 session (3/3 runs) |

Real browsing (YouTube, Google, Facebook over HTTP/3) also works now through TPROXY. `go vet ./app/internal/tproxy/` is clean.
